# Actions and signing

The client saves an intent, prepares it against current indexed/native evidence,
signs and verifies the exact transaction, journals it before sending, then reconciles
its committed result. A timeout or CheckTx acceptance cannot establish success.
This page describes webapp integration `bde1cec8`; a client must deploy its matching
API, schema, generated types and workers together.

## Wallet

`WalletManager` uses CosmJS `DirectSecp256k1HdWallet` with prefix `structs` and a
12-word mnemonic generated from 16 random bytes. It supplies no custom `hdPaths`.
The reference browser stores wallet material in localStorage; that storage is within
the page's trust boundary. See [SAFETY.md](../../SAFETY.md) before adopting its custody
model. Do not put private keys in API bodies, journals or diagnostics.

### Off-chain proof signatures

SHA-256 the UTF-8 bytes of the exact string, sign with secp256k1, and hex-encode the
raw 64-byte R followed by S signature. Public key is compressed 33-byte hex.
These proofs are separate from protobuf transaction signing.

| Use | Signed message |
|---|---|
| Guild proxy signup | `GUILD{guildId}ADDRESS{address}NONCE0` |
| API login/token | `LOGIN_GUILD{guildId}ADDRESS{address}DATETIME{unixTimestamp}` |
| Address registration | Exact preimage below; the separator is one literal pipe |

```text
CHAIN{chainId}|REGISTERADDRESSPLAYER{playerId}ADDRESS{address}NONCE{proofNonce}
```

Login timestamps are canonical decimal strings less than 600 seconds from server
time in either direction. Registration reads the current native address nonce and
requires the target to be unassociated. It also carries the issued activation UUID
through the [device workflow](../../api/webapp/player-address.md). A new proof cannot
replace an uncertain signed registration.

## Signing client and registry

`SigningClientManager` combines CosmJS `defaultRegistryTypes` with generated
`src/js/ts/structs.structs/registry.ts`. The generator pins structsd release
`96cea3a322c406b46ca1feb880dc4497ebd9353f`, its Buf dependency lock and a separate tool
lock. Generate/check through `npm --prefix src run proto:sync -- --source <checkout>`
and `proto:check`, rather than hand-editing generated files.

`forceLong=string` preserves 64-bit protobuf fields. `MessagePayload` validates the
actual generated request schema before persistence and again on restore; unknown
fields and already-rounded unsafe numbers are rejected. Keep integer and coin
amounts as canonical decimal strings. LegacyDec protobuf strings encode scaled
18-place integer atoms, while LCD JSON uses decimal text; the codec adapter handles
that distinction without Number arithmetic.

`creator` is injected from the transaction's fixed signing account when encoding.
A source address, target device or spending owner is a subject, not an alternate
signer. Vault addresses have no private keys. The queue checks account scope again
before preparation and sending.

### Protocol-aware intents

| Intent | Preparation |
|---|---|
| Alpha transfer | Current native ownership/TokenTransfer and vault-first funding with eligible retained collection; selected player resolves to that player's vault, explicit address stays literal |
| Reactor change | Same-height native/indexed complete positions; vault first, then eligible retained addresses deterministically |
| Generator funding | Native target/type/owner/TokenInfuse, vault-first funding with eligible retained collection and current stored output |
| Address registration | Target consent, current nonce/protocol, current signing key and requested grant |
| Device change | Current ownership, nonce lifetime and appropriate permission ceiling; native permission-set/revoke |
| Gameplay | Explicit allowlist for the 17 existing control messages, current signing owner/key bits, native simulation of target/charge/proof rules |

Generated support for a message does not make every low-level builder a reviewed
v0.22 action. A stale primary-address payload is not made vault-aware by new codecs.
Generic queued messages without current-protocol preparation remain deferred.

Reactor withdrawal creates one atomic transaction across at most 16 positions;
it rejects an incomplete request rather than making a partial withdrawal. Native
pagination and request/time budgets are bounded, every batch is simulated, and
ineligible retained stake does not become a fabricated available balance. See
[state-and-data.md](state-and-data.md) for exact read models.

### Fees and exact signed preparation

The legacy `FEE` fallback is zero `ualpha` with gas `500000`. Reviewed gameplay,
registration/device, reactor and generator preparation explicitly use zero `ualpha`
and the release free-gas ceiling `20000000`. A transfer that collects retained funds uses that ceiling too; a single-message transfer retains the fallback.
These are client limits, not proof that arbitrary state will fit or a gas-price rule
for native Cosmos staking messages.

`SigningSubmission.prepare` reads account number/sequence and authority at a pinned
native height, checks the API contract and required projection evidence, then calls
CosmJS `sign` with that explicit account/chain context. Installed CosmJS uses Number
for account number/sequence and query heights; unsupported unsafe values are refused.

The client decodes and checks the wallet's returned message bytes, order, memo,
timeout, fee, mode, signer and signature against the intended transaction. It hashes
the exact TxRaw bytes. Reviewed intents simulate those same signed bytes at the
preparation height; simulation must fit the selected gas limit. Before sending,
protocol and connection/account identity are rechecked. Simulation reserves nothing;
only committed chain execution determines success.

For the configured `structstestnet-111` transition at `3353000`, pre-activation
transactions expire at `3352999`. Post-activation transactions expire at the observed preparation height plus 60 blocks. This client validity window is separate from native permission, staking cooldown and the address-consent proof context.
Other networks require an explicit authoritative configuration.

## The dual-lane queue

`SigningQueueManager` keeps FIFO action and immediate lanes. It selects at most one
new transaction per observed block per address. An eligible charged action has
priority; a blocked action head permits immediate work, including proof completions.
An uncertain submission that can still execute reserves new sends in both lanes. Historical unknown outcomes do not reserve the signing account.

### Sequence numbers and account ownership

Same-origin tabs share a Web Lock keyed by chain and signing account. Inside that
lock the queue reloads the per-intent journal before preparing or sending. A missing
Web Locks implementation or failed durable storage prevents a new send; there is no
unlocked fallback. A secure context with Web Locks is required: localhost was tested; a non-local deployment needs HTTPS and origin-specific acceptance. Different origins/devices need their own account coordination.

Account changes suspend and drain the old queue, persist its evidence under its own
scope, cancel its observers and only then attach the new wallet. A save failure
refuses the handoff. A sequence change elsewhere never proves an old transaction
failed and never authorizes automatically signing its replacement.

### Charge gating

The browser's conservative scheduler/display convention is:

```text
projectedCharge(H) = H - (max(confirmedLastAction, scheduleAnchor) + 1)
```

This client offset is separate from the chain's elapsed-block charge calculation.
The action lane waits until its confirmed last-action source has loaded. A local
optimistic drain affects only display. The anchor advances on a verified successful
charged transaction's inclusion height and disappears when confirmed state catches
up. When charge is short the head waits for another block.

### Persistence

Queue snapshot version 3 uses `signingQueue:{wsUrl}:{address}`. Each intent also has
an independent `signingJournal:{chainId}:{address}:{id}` record. The snapshot cannot
erase signed evidence. Signed bytes/hash and the `prepared` record must be durably
written before the separate `broadcasting` marker; only then can the network send
run. Terminal history is bounded, except records still referenced by saved device-action pointers. Unresolved evidence is never pruned simply for its age.

| Journal/state | Recovery meaning |
|---|---|
| queued / current-format preparing without send evidence | Demonstrably unsent; revalidate before trying |
| prepared journal | Exact bytes saved, but no durable send marker; rebuild only this unsent intent |
| broadcasting / accepted / unknown | May have reached the chain; retain bytes/hash and reconcile only |
| historical / unknown | Legacy record without signed identity, or durable native proof its signed sequence was consumed; preserve the unknown outcome and permit new explicit actions, never replay it |
| succeeded | Matching committed code 0 |
| dropped | Definitive rejection, failure before sending, or proved non-execution after signed expiry |
| cancelled | Explicit cancellation of unsent work |

The 30-minute age limit applies only to unsent intents. Legacy in-flight records
without signed identity remain unknown history and never become fresh sends. They
do not block new explicit actions. Corrupt active queues or journals still block
signing and remain available for recovery. Logout clears private browser state
and closes the unsigned session boundary while retaining public journals.

Legacy lane entries with a nonzero attempt count or recorded broadcast block are
possible sends, even when their status says queued or an earlier import saved them
as version 3. They remain unknown history. The current endpoint/account's `.corrupt`
backup is preserved verbatim. Identifiable possible sends are imported for
observation; malformed backups are not executed and do not reserve the account.
A backup with valid current signed identity still follows native reconciliation.
Unsigned-only backups are not replayed. No notice or new screen is added.
This preserves evidence without resolving an identity-free transaction's outcome
or inspecting another origin's storage. A manually repeated action can execute
again if the earlier action already committed; no automatic repeat is permitted.

### Retries and settlement

There are no automatic signed-send retries. `broadcastTxSync` code 0 is admission,
not completion. A valid CheckTx rejection can settle failure; an ambiguous transport
failure cannot. `find` looks up the original hash and verifies exact bytes, hash,
chain, block/commit identity, transaction index and execution code. A missing hash,
RPC outage or local deadline leaves the result unknown. After exact native TxNotFound, a nonzero signed timeout can settle as dropped only when a later committed snapshot proves the same account number and an unchanged signed account sequence. A passed height alone is insufficient. A later committed snapshot of the same account
with an advanced sequence proves the old signed bytes cannot execute again. Save
that proof durably and release the signing reservation while keeping the outcome
unknown; this is not a failed or successful receipt. Conflicting/unavailable
evidence stays held. Retain the original bytes and proof; never automatically sign
a replacement. Bounded lookups prioritize possible live sends before historical
records and rotate within each group.

`whenSettled(id, signal)` resolves with the terminal transaction; check `status`.
It remains pending for uncertainty. Aborting a view observer rejects only that
observer, not the transaction. Persist the queue ID with the action/work so reload
reattaches to the same operation. `SIGNING_TRANSACTION_SETTLED` notifies observers,
including the authoritative Alpha refresh path.

### Recovering a silently dead signing socket

`OwnedRpcClient` owns the socket and bounds requests. Resume checks use fresh chain
status, share one in-flight probe, respect connection/session epochs and do not
replace the first startup connection. Visibility, focus, pageshow, online and
watchdog paths can recover transport and reconcile journals. A dead socket does
not become a failed payment.

## End to end: building a struct

```text
Existing Deploy control
  → capture gameplay intent and enqueue in the action lane
Block / confirmed charge
  → read API/native authority, sign, verify, simulate exact bytes
  → journal prepared + send marker
  → broadcast once and reconcile original hash
Matching committed success
  → observe indexed work with the original start anchor
  → compute proof using the current catalog/rule epoch
  → queue completion and retain its durable transaction ID
```

Pending visuals are not receipts. Refresh authoritative indexed state after inclusion
and on notification loss/reconnect. The [work lifecycle](work-and-pow.md) keeps local
worker completion distinct from successful native completion.

## Error handling

Keep view, session and action lifetimes separate. Closing an offcanvas cancels its
preview work, while the action observes its persisted transaction. Stale reads and
notifications must not complete a different action or affect a new wallet session.

The existing transfer flow returns a definitive failure to its confirmation screen
with recipient/amount preserved. An unknown send stays protected against duplicates.
Deploy and action controls handle enqueue refusal before adding pending visuals, and release only their own operation lock after a definitive failure. Device and gameplay actions likewise require terminal evidence before reporting
success; a successful self-revoke may clear local state without waiting for an API
read that the revoked key can no longer authenticate.

### Desktop adds a native virtual-player signer

The separately reviewed Desktop source has two additional virtual-player modes.
Its baseline below does not certify compatibility with this webapp integration:

- `sync` / `async` use the Rust ↔ webview bridge and CosmJS.
- `native` / `native_async` sign in Rust and broadcast through LCD REST.

At sign-in, `native_signer_import` can transfer the mnemonic from the webview once. Rust
normalizes it, verifies that `m/44'/118'/0'/0/0` derives the signed-in device address,
stores it in the OS keychain, and retains a zeroized BIP39 seed in memory. A child key at
`m/44'/118'/0'/0/N` is derived per sign and dropped before the first await. Until import
succeeds, native modes fall back to the webview bridge.

Native signing tracks account number/sequence per address, advances on mempool acceptance,
and resets from the chain's expected sequence on disagreement. A per-account mutex is
shared with the JS bridge so modes cannot race one account; `tx_gate_cap` bounds
cross-account concurrency. `native_async` returns after CheckTx acceptance and later emits
`tx_settled`, while `native` waits for inclusion.

This is a custody change, not an MCP key-export feature: tool callers still request
signatures and never receive the mnemonic, but the Rust process and OS keychain now belong
inside the signing trust boundary. See [agent-security.md](../../awareness/agent-security.md).

*Webapp claims verified against integration `bde1cec8`: WalletManager,
SigningClientManager, SigningQueueManager, SigningSubmission, TransactionJournal,
SigningTransaction, MessagePayload, protocol/fee constants and intent preparation.
The checked release fixtures include exact signed bytes, simulation, native atomic
rollback, reload/unknown outcomes and unchanged rendered controls.*

*Desktop integration retains its separate verification against
`3f04437d5606d6736df41301bb980893129a7912`: `mcp/native_signer.rs`,
`vplayer_bridge.rs`, `tx_gate.rs`, `tx_retry.rs`, and `tools/system.rs`. No new Desktop
compatibility or deployment claim is made here.*

</document>

# Work and proof-of-work

The browser hashes current authoritative work with its original chain anchor.
Finding a hash and confirming its completion transaction are separate lifecycles.
This page describes integration `581fcd0f`; protocol rules come from structsd release
`96cea3a`. See [hashing](../../knowledge/mechanics/hashing.md) for the CLI/mechanics.

## The hash

Use one SHA-256 pass over the exact UTF-8 input and a lowercase hex digest:

```text
{structId}{BUILD|MINE|REFINE}{originalBlockStart}NONCE{nonce}
{fleetId}@{planetId}RAID{originalBlockStart}NONCE{nonce}
```

The braces and choice bars are notation, not bytes. There are no other separators.
`TaskStateFactory` preserves exact start/difficulty strings and builds the prefix;
postfix is empty. Examples for nonce `42` are `5-1BUILD3352900NONCE42`,
`5-2MINE3352900NONCE42`, `5-3REFINE3352900NONCE42` and
`9-1@2-10RAID3352900NONCE42`.

`js-sha256` runs in a dedicated worker. Nonces begin at a random offset; workers do
not partition ranges. A digest's leading zero count is checked against the required
number of hexadecimal zeroes. Before submission, recompute the hash from the expected
identity/prefix and nonce, not a worker's claimed result alone.

## Difficulty decays, so waiting is cheaper than working

For observed age `a` and difficulty range `r`, v0.22 uses integer arithmetic:

```text
if a <= 1 or r <= 1: difficulty = 64
otherwise: difficulty = 64 - max{k in [0,63] : r^k <= a^63}
```

`integerWorkDifficulty` uses BigInt and at most 63 products, matching the release's
`CalculateDifficulty`. Do not use floating logarithms for eligibility: a boundary
rounding difference can change the required leading-zero count.

`workDifficultyAtHeight` chooses the configured rule using an observed chain height.
It refuses a zero anchor or a height before the anchor. The scheduled testnet boundary
is `3353000`; a task started before it keeps that same original start height while
adopting current difficulty rules and current type data. Resetting the anchor to the
upgrade height creates a different proof input.

The wall-clock estimate (nominal six-second blocks) is for progress/ETA only. It cannot
wake a waiting worker or make its proof eligible. Block/rule messages supply the
checkpoint used by `getCurrentDifficulty()`.

### The idle policy

The browser waits until difficulty is at most 10, unless explicitly forced. That is
a CPU policy, not a chain requirement: ten leading hex zeroes take roughly 2^40
attempts in expectation. The CLI guidance uses `-D 3` for lower compute cost. Neither
setting changes native verification.

## The worker loop

The worker hashes at most 4096 candidates per batch, yields to process messages,
and schedules another batch with MessageChannel. This avoids nested `setTimeout(0)` clamping while still allowing control messages between batches. This bounds how long a height/rule/cancellation update
waits behind hashing. It publishes progress every five million iterations and on
important state changes. A previously found candidate is reusable only if its hash
still satisfies the current observed-height rule.

`TaskProcess` and `TaskWorker` exchange `version: "work-v022-1"`, a monotonically
increasing revision, and `start`/`update` messages. A wrong-version reply fails the
worker; no handshake within ten seconds does too. Replies from replaced workers or
older revisions cannot replace current task state or submit a proof.

### Same object, new rules

The process ID is the object ID, so process existence alone does not establish that
its work is current. Full identity includes object, category, raid target, original
anchor and prefix. When only rules or observed height change, update the same worker
and preserve its searched nonces/candidate. Reject older rule snapshots. When the
work identity changes, replace the worker; a late reply from the old one is ignored.

The manager caps active processes at five and starts after the existing eight-second
startup delay. These controls and progress displays remain unchanged.

### Ore clocks and raids

Mining/refining anchors belong to the planet. Each eligible extractor/refinery gets
its own struct-bound proof using the shared anchor. Native-chain notifications prompt
a fresh scoped work read; their unversioned values do not replace the API anchor.
A complete accepted snapshot determines which structs still have work.

An incoming raid stops local mine/refine hashing. The manager reconciles after the
raid using current clocks/work; it does not reassign a new start height based on the
browser's receive time. Raid completion work also depends on the target's shield
state. A work removal can discard a local candidate, but never its signed journal.

## Restoring after a reload

`GET /api/work/player/{id}` supplies the ready `work` projection and coherent source
metadata. `WorkFactory` validates owner, category, object/raid-target identity and
exact uint64 anchor/difficulty strings. Empty complete snapshots retain metadata and
can authorize removals; a failed or incomplete read cannot.

Partial hashing progress is not durably saved, so an unsent search restarts. A queued
or signed completion is different: `WorkSubmission` matches its expected object,
category, raid target and original anchor through the actual proof hash. For a signed
submission it decodes the durable bytes, which outrank a mutable saved payload.
Reattach the observer to that queue ID instead of generating another completion.

`WorkRefreshManager` periodically refreshes catalog and work, including reconnect,
resume and activation boundaries. Older/conflicting snapshots and responses for a
replaced player/session are refused. Existing type-object references update in place
so open controls see the new catalog without a new UI.

## Completion

| Work | Native message | Fields after creator injection |
|---|---|---|
| Build | `MsgStructBuildComplete` | `structId`, `proof`, `nonce` |
| Mine | `MsgStructOreMinerComplete` | `structId`, `proof`, `nonce` |
| Refine | `MsgStructOreRefineryComplete` | `structId`, `proof`, `nonce` |
| Raid | `MsgPlanetRaidComplete` | `fleetId`, `proof`, `nonce` |

Proof and nonce are strings. Raid target remains bound by the proof input and current
fleet state even though the completion message carries no separate target field.
These reviewed gameplay intents use the immediate queue lane and exact signed
simulation before sending.

A successful committed completion suppresses hashing of the same stale work. An
unknown send only reconciles its original transaction. A definitive failure permits
another automatic hashing attempt only after a newer complete work snapshot. If
storage or queue pressure prevents enqueueing, the unsent completed candidate remains
in memory for a later block; it is not silently reported as submitted.

The view's observer can be cancelled without cancelling a send. Logout stops workers,
clears observers and closes the session boundary while retaining signed transaction
evidence. Tutorial work remains simulated and cannot enter the native queue.

## Deployment and verification

Production HTML selects the fingerprinted application bundle through its asset
manifest; that bundle references its fingerprinted worker chunk. Deploy matching
assets together and retain needed old hashed assets for already-open pages. The
version/revision handshake prevents an incompatible worker from submitting results;
a reload alone is not proof that all tabs adopted the new application.

The source suites cover exact integer boundaries, same-process rule changes, old
worker replies, original anchors, stale work, unknown/failed/committed submissions,
and logout. Native release fixtures and rendered isolated build/tutorial checks are
separate evidence. Keep those distinctions when reporting client acceptance.

*Verified against webapp `581fcd0f`: TaskManager, TaskProcess, TaskState,
TaskStateFactory, TaskWorker, WorkFactory, WorkDifficulty, WorkSubmission,
WorkRefreshManager and TaskConstants. Integer eligibility cross-checked directly
against release `x/structs/types/work.go`; no chain checkout was modified.*

</document>

# Real-time events with GRASS

GRASS transports committed database notifications through NATS. Use them to request
current state and drive captured activity; they are not a durable transaction receipt
or a complete balance history. The reference browser keeps its existing UI while
refresh managers reconcile funds, work and signing authority.

## Connection

`GrassManager` uses `@nats-io/nats-core` `wsconnect`. The stock browser constructs two
managers at `ws://{hostname}:1443`, without NATS credentials:

| Manager | Subscription | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `grassManager` | `structs.>` | Game and device notifications |
| `blockGrassManager` | `consensus` | Observed block clock |

Other clients discover the advertised guild service and its auth/TLS requirements;
do not infer a public host's current availability or rewrite its URL scheme.

NATS retries transient disconnections indefinitely with a two-second reconnect wait.
The outer supervisor handles closed/failed streams with backoff from one to thirty
seconds. Listener registrations survive reconnect. Resume/watchdog checks use the
shared consensus clock to detect a stale connection and avoid duplicate reconnects.
A quiet game subject alone does not mean the connection is dead.

Initial connection and NATS reconnect status dispatch `GRASS_CONNECTED`. Funds,
work and authority refresh managers use that signal for fresh reads. No new status
screen is implied. Core NATS does not backfill the gap merely because a socket
reconnected.

## One subscription, client-side filtering

Each manager has one NATS subscription. `GrassManager` decodes JSON, requires envelope
`subject` and `category`, then fans out to registered listeners. Listeners filter
scope/category themselves. Use narrower subjects for a custom client that does not
need the reference browser's broad subscription.

Representative reviewed paths:

| Subject | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `consensus` | Block notifications, independent of activity hydration |
| `structs.player.{guild_id}.{player_id}` | Player and indexed address updates |
| `structs.planet.{planet_id}.{player_id}` | Struct/combat/fleet/raid activity |
| `structs.grid.{object_type}.{object_id}.{player_id}` | Grid attribute notification |
| `structs.inventory.{denom}.{guild_id}.{player_id}.{address}` | Ledger invalidation with canonical owner metadata |
| `structs.grid.player.{owner_id}` | Player infusion invalidation |
| `structs.grid.guild.{owner_id}` | Guild infusion invalidation |
| `structs.address.register.{code}` | Pending consent for an existing player's new device |
| `structs.guild.{guild_id}` | Guild consensus/meta/membership-application notification |

Unresolved ownership can use `noPlayer`/`noGuild`. A guild vault's owner remains the
guild, not its leader. Dotted synthetic denominations create extra NATS tokens, so
do not parse inventory ownership by a fixed token offset. `*` matches one token;
`>` matches trailing tokens. Planet observers use `structs.planet.{planet_id}.*`.

Struct activity lives on the planet path; the reviewed triggers do not provide
separate `structs.struct.{id}` or `structs.fleet.{id}` activity subscriptions.
`consensus` is the block subscription, not `structs.global`.

## The listener contract

A listener supplies a unique `name`, synchronous `handler(messageData)` and optional
`shouldUnregister()`. Names are Map keys; re-registering a name replaces that listener.
Unregistration is checked immediately after the handler returns. Async work inside
a listener still needs its own stale-context/cancellation checks; a flag set later
is noticed on a later dispatch.

Current listener groups include:

| Group | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Block and last action | Update observed height and confirmed charge base |
| Player load/capacity/ore/shields | Update established display/state paths |
| `PlayerAlphaListener`, `AlphaChangeListener` | Request authoritative funds refresh; never apply balance deltas |
| `StructListener` | Refresh structs, reconcile build work, and render ordered combat effects |
| Mine/refine status listeners | Request current scoped work reconciliation |
| Raid/planet raid listeners | Maintain offensive/defensive raid state and relevant local work |
| Player created/new planet | Continue scoped onboarding/entity loading |
| Address revoked | Request a native ownership check for the active key, or refresh another device's list |

Economic/device completion is owned by its transaction observer and current evidence,
not the first similar-looking notification. Removed one-shot transfer/infusion/device
listeners are not an integration API to copy.

`RegistrationRefreshListener` gives pending-consent and registration-status observers a prompt read wakeup. It matches the current activation/device context, coalesces bursts and in-flight reads, and spaces notification-driven reads by at least one second. Polling still backs off from two to thirty seconds if notifications are lost. A wakeup never establishes successful approval or substitutes for the exact native nonce/owner and indexed association checks. Aborted observers unregister and cancel their timers.

## Refresh committed funds and work

`AlphaChangeListener` matches the current owner on inventory subjects and on explicit
infusion invalidations. It requests `AlphaRefreshManager` through
`block_height_exact` (or a supported legacy height). `PlayerAlphaListener` also
invalidates rather than assigning an unqualified grid balance.

The ledger trigger carries `amount_p_exact`, `id_exact`, `block_height_exact`,
canonical `owner_type`/`owner_id`/`is_vault` and counterparty ownership. Those fields
preserve precision; they do not establish that a client has every preceding event.
Infusion changes notify old/new/live owners with `invalidates: "infusion"`, including
reassignment and deletion. Refetch exact available-funds evidence and complete positions; a retained native refund is an invalidation, not permission to run a background sweep.

`AlphaRefreshManager` coalesces notifications, checks monotonic source heights, and
refreshes on resume/reconnect and visible polling. Work/catalog refresh similarly
uses coherent snapshots rather than notification anchors. `SessionAuthorityManager`
checks native ownership before treating a key as revoked. See
[state-and-data.md](state-and-data.md) for each manager's scope and cadence.

## Hydrate large planet activity before dispatch

PostgreSQL NOTIFY payloads are limited to 8 KB. A large attack can be a keyed stub
with `stub: true` or `stub: "true"`, carrying `planet_id`, `seq`, `time`, category
and subject without `detail`. The release's multi-target/projectile fixture exercises
this path through the actual writer, database, bridge and browser.

Fetch the exact row using the authenticated endpoint:

```text
GET /api/planet-activity/planet/{planet_id}/event/{seq}?time={URL-encoded-original-time}
```

Preserve the original timestamp string, microseconds and timezone. JavaScript Date
round-trips lose needed precision. The endpoint returns an object-valued `detail`
or null for a missing exact row. Match the full key and category; never substitute
the latest activity row.

`resolvePlanetActivityNotification` fetches only for a currently observed player and
planet, and discards late replies after session/account/planet changes.
`GrassManager` awaits hydration before dispatching the next message on that stream,
then also checks the connection identity. The independent consensus subscription
continues. Missing/malformed detail is skipped as unavailable, not converted into
an empty successful attack. General async listener work still is not globally ordered.

## Combat playback

Typed attack detail supplies rolled projectile damage, final net volley damage and
observed health; they are not interchangeable. A target can counter and then die from
the attacker's explosion. Render the counter at its intermediate health before the
later destruction, including blocked/evaded cases. Do not apply effect damage again
to indexed models; refresh involved structs.

A zero-health activity row is not guaranteed, so combine status/current-state reads
with attack detail. The [captured event reference](../../api/streaming/event-schemas.md)
and [exact event endpoint](../../api/webapp/planet-activity.md#exact-event-lookup)
define those payloads. The renderer fixture verifies actual animation completion,
queue drainage and final health for counter/rebound and large-event cases.

## What the stream will not do for you

- It has no durable replay or global client deduplication/gap recovery.
- Notification order is not a replacement for coherent SQL/native source heights.
- A balance, attack or address event does not prove an unrelated signed transaction
  committed. Match its durable hash/bytes and native execution result first.
- A connection event does not certify all displayed data as current. Reconcile the
  required scoped models, honoring incomplete/unavailable responses.
- Stale notifications or failed reads do not authorize a new send, reset a proof's
  original anchor, or erase a local key.

*Verified against webapp `581fcd0f`: GrassManager, PlanetActivityNotification,
AlphaChangeListener, PlayerAddressRevokedListener, current listener registration and
scoped refresh managers. Subject/ownership paths were checked against structs-pg
`400e1c1` and the bridge forwarding logic. Captured release-event transport and real
rendered hydration are separate from live deployment acceptance.*

</document>

<source>develop/client/rendering-entities.md</source>
---
description: "How players and structs are drawn: layered profile-picture compositing, struct art selection, and the Lottie animation queue."
---

# Rendering entities

**Purpose**: How players and structs are drawn — layered PFP compositing, struct art
selection, the Lottie lifecycle, and the queue that keeps combat animations coherent.

---

## Profile pictures

A player's avatar is not an image file. It is **five PNG layers composited by index**,
painted back to front: background, arms, body, neck, head.

```js
// src/js/view_models/components/PfpViewerComponent.js
const layers = [
  ['background', this.pfp.background],
  ['arms', this.pfp.arms],
  ['body', this.pfp.body],
  ['neck', this.pfp.neck],
  ['head', this.pfp.head],
];

return layers
  .filter(([, index]) => index !== null && index !== undefined)
  .map(([part, index]) =>
    `<img class="pfp-viewer-layer" src="/img/pfp/${part}/pfp_${part}_${index}.png" alt="">`
  )
  .join('');
```

Path convention is `/img/pfp/{part}/pfp_{part}_{index}.png`. All five layers are absolutely
positioned at 72×72 in the portrait container, so later DOM nodes paint on top.

Indices are **1-based** and bounded by:

```js
// src/js/constants/PfpConstants.js
head: 87, neck: 10, body: 57, arms: 34, background: 6
```

That is 87 × 10 × 57 × 34 × 6 ≈ 10.1 million combinations from 194 assets.

The indices live on the player as `pfp_client_render_attributes`, parsed from chain data
by `PlayerFactory`. Note the trap: `Player` also has a `pfp` string field that is **not
used for rendering**. Reading it and expecting an image URL is a natural mistake.

Two fallback behaviours, and one gap:

- No attributes at all, or unparseable JSON → `/img/portrait-placeholder.png`.
- An individual layer index that is `null` → that layer is skipped.
- **An out-of-range index is not validated.** The browser requests a URL that doesn't
  exist and you get a broken image. Clamp against `PFP_PART_COUNTS` yourself.

Rendering a PFP requires no network call beyond the layer PNGs, which makes it cheap to
show avatars in a long roster. Randomising one at signup is `Math.floor(Math.random() *
count) + 1` per layer.

---

## Struct art

Two rendering modes, and the choice between them is about state, not about quality.

| Mode | Used for |
|---|---|
| **Static still** — layered PNGs | Resting appearance on a map tile |
| **Lottie animation** — SVG | Combat, deployment, movement, stealth, destruction, active loops |

### Stills

`StructTypeArtSetBuilder` maps each struct type to its PNG layers under `/img/structs`:

```js
buildCruiser(structType) {
  const art = new StructTypeArtSet(structType);
  art[STRUCT_STILL_LAYERS.STRUCT_VARIANT_BASE]  = this.structImageDir + '/cruiser/cruiser-struct-base.png';
  art[STRUCT_STILL_LAYERS.STRUCT_VARIANT_DMG]   = this.structImageDir + '/cruiser/cruiser-struct-dmg.png';
  art[STRUCT_WEAPON_SYSTEM.PRIMARY_WEAPON]      = this.structImageDir + '/cruiser/cruiser-top-weapon-ballistic.png';
  art[STRUCT_WEAPON_SYSTEM.SECONDARY_WEAPON]    = this.structImageDir + '/cruiser/cruiser-top-weapon-smart.png';
  art[STRUCT_WATER_RIPPLE]                      = this.structImageDir + '/cruiser/cruiser-bottom-ripples.png';
  return art;
}
```

Variant selection is driven by health, with per-type layout differences — a Frigate puts
its primary weapon on the bottom detail layer, a Cruiser on top:

```js
renderHTML(currentHealth = -1, structVariant = '') {
  if (currentHealth === 0) {
    return `<div class="struct-still"></div>`;      // destroyed: nothing
  }
  if (structVariant === '') {
    structVariant = (0 < currentHealth && currentHealth < this.structType.max_health)
      ? STRUCT_STILL_LAYERS.STRUCT_VARIANT_DMG
      : STRUCT_STILL_LAYERS.STRUCT_VARIANT_BASE;
  }
  return `
    <div class="struct-still">
      ${this.renderTopDetailLayers(structVariant)}
      ${this.renderStructVariant(structVariant)}
      ${this.renderBottomDetailLayers(structVariant)}
    </div>
  `;
}
```

Three z-index bands order the layers: bottom detail 100, body 200, top detail 300.

Stealth is handled two ways. Most types get 50% opacity via `struct-stealth-active`; a
Submersible swaps to a dedicated `STRUCT_VARIANT_HIDDEN` sprite, because a half-transparent
submarine is not the same idea as a submerged one.

Note that `StructTypeArtSetBuilder` has no art set for Continental Power Plant or World
Engine, and will throw if asked for one. Those types presumably never reach a tactical
map, but guard for it if your surface is more general.

### Lottie

`lottie-web` 5.12.2, loaded from `/js/vendor/`, always with the SVG renderer. Animation
JSON lives at predictable paths:

```
/lottie/deployment_{space|air|land|water}/data.json      shared by ambit
/lottie/attack_primary_weapon/{snake_case_type}/data.json    per struct type
/lottie/stealth_activate/{snake_case_type}/data.json         per struct type
```

The still and the animation are mutually exclusive: playing an animation hides the still
container. Online extractors/refineries use an active loop while their ore work is
not halted by a raid; a halted loop returns to its still until authoritative state
permits work again.

**Lottie lifecycle is where the memory leaks are**, and the reference client is explicit
about it:

```js
/**
 * Tear down all lottie players owned by this viewer. Must be called before
 * the viewer is dereferenced (e.g. when its tile is cleared or the viewer
 * is replaced), otherwise lottie-web's internal animation registry keeps
 * the JSON, image bitmaps, rAF subscription, and DOM listeners alive.
 */
```

Dropping the reference is not enough — `lottie-web` holds its own registry. The teardown
chain is `MapStructViewerComponent.destroy()` → `lottieCustomPlayer.destroyAll()` →
`animation.destroy()`, and the map layer calls it **before** overwriting a tile, not
after.

Animations load lazily on first play. During playback the client swaps struct PNGs into
named SVG placeholders (`.struct_init`, `.struct_top_layer_1`), using a generation counter
so a stale async swap from a previous animation cannot land on the current one.

---

## The animation event queue

A single attack produces a burst of GRASS events: the attacker fires, the defender
evades, a point-defence cannon counters, a struct takes damage, a struct is destroyed.
Played concurrently, they trample each other's partial state — health bars and still
images end up showing a mixture of moments that never existed.

`AnimationEventQueue` serialises them globally. One animation plays at a time, and the
next starts only when the previous reports it has ended:

```js
// src/js/data_structures/AnimationEventQueue.js
enqueue(event) {
  super.enqueue(event);
  if (!this.isPlaying) {
    this.playNext();
  }
}

playNext() {
  if (this.isEmpty()) {
    const wasPlaying = this.isPlaying;
    this.isPlaying = false;
    this.currentEvent = null;
    if (wasPlaying) {
      window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent(EVENTS.ANIMATION_QUEUE_EMPTY));
    }
    return;
  }
  this.isPlaying = true;
  this.currentEvent = super.dequeue();
  window.dispatchEvent(this.currentEvent);
}
```

`StructListener.handleStructAttack` expands one `struct_attack` message into an ordered
list of `AnimationEvent`s and enqueues them in narrative order.

Three consequences ripple outward from this design, and each is worth copying:

**Game state and displayed state diverge on purpose.** Refreshes bring `gameState`
to authoritative post-attack values, while queued animation events carry
`options.healthAfter` for the intermediate moment. Do not write those temporary
values back over final indexed state. The bars catch up as the sequence plays.

A reported target counter plays even when rebound later destroys that target. Show
volley damage, then the counter, then rebound and final destruction. A blocked or
evaded volley does not damage the target; net volley damage is carried on the final
projectile row. Preserve the release flags and defense metadata, rather than
inferring that a final destroyed flag means the earlier counter never happened.
Every participant is refreshed, including countering defenders. Large notification
stubs must first resolve by exact event identity, preserving per-planet order; see
[GRASS](realtime-grass.md).

**Other renderers defer to the queue.** The HUD layer holds back struct-HUD renders while
an animation is playing and flushes them on `ANIMATION_QUEUE_EMPTY`:

```js
if (this.gameState.animationEventQueue && this.gameState.animationEventQueue.isPlaying) {
  this.deferredHudRenders.set(event.struct.id, event.struct);
  return;
}
```

`StructManager` likewise skips showing a still while `isStructAnimating(struct.id)`, so a
routine refresh cannot tear down a Lottie mid-play.

**Chained side effects hang off `onAnimationEnd`.** A move sequence clears the old tile
and refreshes the struct after the departure animation and before the arrival one, which
is the only way to get that ordering right.

**The still after an animation comes from current struct state.** The viewer restores a
Submersible's hidden art from `struct.isHidden()` after ordinary animations; only the
stealth activate/deactivate animations override that value while their confirming state
event is still in flight. Low-orbit ballistic interception also has its own evade Lottie,
and the Cruiser primary uses the delayed-impact sequence against both land and water
targets.

Deployment animations are the exception: they autoplay when a struct first renders after
being built, bypassing the queue entirely, because nothing else is competing at that
moment.

---

*Verified against structs-webapp `ae4457e2` (2026-10-30):
`src/js/view_models/components/PfpViewerComponent.js`, `StructStillRenderer.js`,
`MapStructViewerComponent.js`, `MapStructLottieAnimationSVG.js`,
`src/js/data_structures/AnimationEventQueue.js`, and
`src/js/factories/AnimationEventFactory.js`.*

---
title: The tactical map in a Structs client
description: "How the tactical map is built: the ambit stack, the tile grid, fog of war, and the picture-in-picture trick that keeps combat visible."
---

# The tactical map in a Structs client

**Purpose**: How the tactical map is built — the ambit stack, the tile grid, fog of war,
and the picture-in-picture trick that keeps combat visible while you scroll.

---

## It's DOM, not canvas

The whole map is nested `<div>` elements with CSS background sprites. No canvas, no WebGL.
That sounds naive for a game map and turns out to be the right call: tiles are 128×128
pixel art on a fixed grid, the whole thing scales with a CSS `transform`, and every tile
is inspectable and event-targetable for free.

Seven stacked layers:

```js
// src/js/view_models/components/map/MapComponent.js
return `
  <div id="${this.mapId}" class="map">
    <div id="${this.terrainId}" class="map-terrain"></div>
    <div id="${this.ornamentsId}" class="map-ornaments"></div>
    <div id="${this.markersId}" class="map-markers"></div>
    <div id="${this.structLayerId}" class="map-struct-layer"></div>
    <div id="${this.structHUDLayerId}" class="map-struct-hud-layer"></div>
    <div id="${this.fogOfWarId}" class="map-fog-of-war-anchor"></div>
    <div id="${this.tileSelectionId}" class="map-tile-selection"></div>
  </div>
`;
```

Terrain, structs and struct HUD all share identical row and column geometry, so a tile at
grid position (row, col) means the same place in all three. Tile size is 128×128,
matching `--tile-width` and `--tile-height` in `sui.css`.

---

## The ambit stack

Only ambits the planet actually has are rendered — the planet's slot counts decide — and
they always stack in the same order, top to bottom: **space, air, land, water**.

```js
// src/js/models/Planet.js
getAmbits() {
  const ambits = [];
  if (this.space_slots && this.space_slots > 0) { ambits.push(AMBITS.SPACE); }
  if (this.air_slots   && this.air_slots   > 0) { ambits.push(AMBITS.AIR); }
  // … land, water
}
```

`.map-terrain` is a column flexbox, so DOM order is visual order. Each ambit is two rows
of tiles (`MAP_TILE_ROWS_PER_AMBIT = 2`).

### Transitions between ambits

Between every pair of ambits — and after the last one — sits a 128px transition band, so
the map reads as a continuous vertical slice of a world rather than as stacked strips:

```js
for (let i = 0; i < ambits.length; i++) {
  let transition = this.transitionBuilder.make(this.mapColCount, lastAmbit, ambits[i]);
  html += transition.renderHTML();
  html += (new MapTerrainAmbitComponent(…)).renderHTML();
  if (i === ambits.length - 1) {
    transition = this.transitionBuilder.make(this.mapColCount, ambits[i]);
    html += transition.renderHTML();
  }
}
```

Some transitions are named rather than generic — entering land gets a `HORIZON` band.

The struct and HUD layers insert their own transition rows at the same offsets, tagged
`data-tile-type="TRANSITION"`, purely to keep the three grids aligned.

---

## Tiles

Terrain tile classes encode ambit plus position within the ambit block:

```js
// src/js/util/TileClassNameUtil.js
getTileClassName(ambit, verticalPos, horizontalPos) {
  return `tile-${ambit.toLowerCase()}-${verticalPos}-${horizontalPos}`;
}
```

Vertical is `top`/`middle`/`bottom`, horizontal is `left`/`middle`/`right`, giving classes
like `.tile-space-top-left` backed by `/img/tiles/space/space-1-1-top-left.png`. Edge
variants (`tile-{ambit}-edge-…`, `tile-horizon-…`) handle the transition bands.

Struct-layer tiles carry their identity in data attributes rather than in classes, which
is what makes hit-testing a click trivial:

```html
<div class="map-struct-layer-tile mod-side-left"
     data-tile-type="PLANETARY_SLOT"
     data-side="left"
     data-player-id="4-118"
     data-ambit="land"
     data-slot="2"
     data-struct-id=""></div>
```

Columns run: defender command ship, planetary slots, defender fleet, a divider, attacker
fleet, attacker command ship. Attacker-side tiles are mirrored with a single CSS rule:

```css
.map-struct-layer-tile.mod-side-right { transform: scaleX(-1); }
```

---

## Fog of war

Two mechanisms for the same idea, applied at different layers.

**An overlay** covers everything from the divider rightwards, but only when you are
looking at your own planet with no attacker present:

```js
shouldDisplayFogOfWar() {
  return !this.attacker && (this.perspective === MAP_PERSPECTIVES.DEFENDER);
}
```

It is a left edge sprite plus a repeating body, sized in pixels from the divider position.

**Fog tiles** replace attacker-side struct tiles with `data-tile-type="FOG_OF_WAR"`
carrying `icon-unknown-territory`. These hold the grid positions so geometry stays
consistent, while making the tiles non-interactive and visibly unknown.

The distinction matters when you are building a scouting or intel view: the overlay is
cosmetic, the tile type is what your click handling should key off.

---

## The struct layer

`MapStructLayerComponent.renderStruct()` resolves a tile's `data-*` attributes to a struct
and then takes one of three paths: no struct → destroy any old viewer and clear the tile;
unbuilt struct → show the deployment indicator; built struct → create a
`MapStructViewerComponent` and mount it.

Planetary tile lookup also requires the struct's `location_id` to match the map's planet, preventing a same-owner/same-slot struct on another planet from landing here.

**The old viewer is always destroyed before the tile is overwritten**, for the Lottie
reasons in [rendering-entities.md](rendering-entities.md#lottie).

Updates arrive as `window` CustomEvents, so the map never polls:

| Event | Effect |
|---|---|
| `RENDER_ALL_STRUCTS` | Full resync |
| `RENDER_STRUCT` | Re-render one struct |
| `ANIMATION` | Play a queued animation on the matching viewer |
| `RENDER_DEPLOYMENT_INDICATOR` | Show the building indicator |
| `CLEAR_STRUCT_TILE` | Clear |
| `SHOW`/`CLEAR_DEFEND_TARGETS`, `SHOW`/`CLEAR_ATTACK_TARGETS` | Targeting highlights |

The chain of custody for a live update is worth tracing once:
GRASS → `StructListener` → `StructManager.refreshStruct()` → `RenderStructEvent` or an
enqueued animation → the map layer.

### Selection, targeting, and power state

Selection is a separate transparent anchor grid above the art. Selecting a struct causes
its HUD status context to dominate: unrelated destroyed/offline/overloaded indicators
are hidden, while the selected struct's defender/protected relationships remain visible.
Raid-halted extractor/refinery work uses the attention indicator and pauses its active
loop; raid-status events refresh these views while leaving queued animations intact.
Offline structs use the 32px `energy-deactivated` sprite; an online struct whose owner is
overloaded uses `no-power`.

Attack target validity is recomputed while choosing a target, including when stealth
changes. Only the active map is repainted, avoiding stale invalid-selection marks on the
other still-mounted map. During attack, move or defense target selection, an invalid
or empty tile keeps the current source/selection mode; cancellation comes from the
action control. A valid selection plays an 800 ms target indicator: enemy, friendly
or neutral. Preloaded blobs receive per-play object URLs that are revoked on cleanup.
The indicator confirms selection, not native execution.

### Mouse drag panning

One document-level `MapPanController` pans every `.map-container` by scrolling the
window opposite the mouse delta. It starts only after a 5px threshold, captures the
pointer, suppresses the click that ends a pan, prevents native anchor dragging, and uses
viewport pixels so movement stays 1:1 under the 2×/4× CSS map scale. Touch and pen retain
native drag scrolling.

---

## Picture-in-picture

A neat solution to a real problem. The map is larger than the viewport and scaled with a
CSS `transform`, so during a combat sequence the struct that is currently animating may be
entirely off-screen — you hear about a battle you cannot see.

`MapPictureInPictureComponent` is a fixed 128×128 viewport appended to `document.body`
(outside the scaled container, so it can position against the viewport) that mirrors the
animating struct whenever its real tile is fully off-screen. It slides in from whichever
side the struct is on, tracks visibility on scroll and resize, and slides out when the
[animation queue](rendering-entities.md#the-animation-event-queue) drains.

Each PIP is scoped to its owning `mapId` and struct-layer container. Hidden maps are
ignored, so an animation on the background map cannot open its bubble on the visible
map. Counter and block animations carry badges because a single-struct PIP lacks the
other participant that explains the action.

The critical detail is one flag:

```
 * The PIP's struct viewer runs in "muted" mode (no `AnimationEndEvent`
 * dispatch) so its lottie completions can't drive the global
 * `AnimationEventQueue`.
```

Two viewers play the same animation, so without muting, the queue would advance twice per
event and the sequence would run at double speed and then desynchronise. Any time you
mirror an animation, mute the copy.

---

*Verified against structs-webapp `ae4457e2` (2026-10-30):
`src/js/view_models/components/map/`, `src/js/util/TileClassNameUtil.js`,
`src/js/models/Planet.js`, and `src/js/framework/MapPanController.js`.*

</document>

<source>develop/client/desktop-extensions.md</source>
---
description: "How to add capability to Structs Desktop: a new MCP tool, a new board page, serving SUI over HTTP, or agent-driven UI."
---

# Extending Structs Desktop

**Purpose**: How to add capability to [structs-desktop](../repos.md) — a new MCP tool, a
new board page, or agent-driven UI — rather than how to use what's already there.

For *using* the existing tools, see [TOOLS.md](../../TOOLS.md) and
[knowledge/infrastructure/structs-desktop.md](../../knowledge/infrastructure/structs-desktop.md).

Structs Desktop is Tauri 2: a Rust backend (`src-tauri/`) hosting an embedded MCP server,
and a webview frontend (`frontend/`) built on [SUI](../ui/index.md). The two halves are
worth understanding separately, because most contributions touch only one.

---

## Adding an MCP tool

Tools live in `src-tauri/src/mcp/tools/`, one module per surface:

```
action.rs   board.rs      board_pages.rs  dashboard.rs  doctrine.rs
events.rs   format.rs     hasher.rs       intel.rs      map.rs
mass_action.rs  players.rs  policy.rs     sequence.rs   strike.rs  system.rs
```

They surface as exactly 13 advertised tools: `structs_action`, `structs_dashboard`,
`structs_hash`, `structs_intel`, `structs_policy`, `structs_events`,
`structs_sequence`, `structs_players`, `structs_map`, `structs_board`,
`structs_doctrine`, `structs_strike`, and `structs_system`. Agent-driven components
belong to `structs_board`; `structs_ui` is only a retired-call migration stub.

The shape to follow is **one tool per surface with an operation parameter**, not one tool
per operation. `structs_action` covers every game action rather than exposing forty
separate build/move/attack tools. That keeps the tool list legible to a model — which is
the actual constraint, since a long flat tool list degrades selection accuracy.

Around the tools sit the pieces that make them safe and fast, and a new tool should reuse
rather than reimplement them:

| Module | Provides |
|---|---|
| `tx_queue.rs`, `tx_retry.rs`, `txq_bridge.rs` | Transaction queueing and retry — the same serialise-don't-track-sequences discipline as the [webapp queue](actions-and-signing.md#the-dual-lane-queue) |
| `policy.rs` | Capability gating. Anything that signs must pass policy |
| `error_translator.rs` | Chain errors into text an agent can act on |
| `enrich.rs`, `roster_cache.rs` | Resolving IDs to names without a round trip per lookup |
| `event_buffer.rs`, `board_feed.rs` | The event stream behind the board |
| `telemetry.rs`, `watchdog.rs` | Health and liveness |

The automation loops (`auto_build.rs`, `auto_harvest.rs`, `auto_defend.rs`,
`auto_raid.rs`, `auto_infuse.rs`, `auto_response.rs`) are the closest thing to worked
examples of a long-running background capability, and `loop_util.rs` holds the shared
cadence machinery.

---

## Adding a board page

The Team Ops board (`frontend/board.html` + `board.js` + `board-pages.js`) is a
six-area operations console built entirely on SUI: Command, Armada, Industry,
War, Explore, and System. Terminal is a customizable card workspace and Comms is
Matrix-backed. Pages still self-register:

```js
Board.registerPage = function (name, def) {
  def = def || {};
  def.lastRun = 0;
  Board.pages[name] = def;
};
```

A page definition is small:

```js
Board.registerPage('energy', {
  refresh: renderEnergy,
  cadenceMs: 30000,
  onEnter: renderEnergy,
});
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `refresh` | Called on the cadence while the page is visible. Return a promise if async |
| `cadenceMs` | How often. Existing pages range from 2.5s (`tx`) to 30s (`energy`) |
| `onEnter` | Called once when the page becomes visible — usually the same function, for an immediate paint |

**Pick the cadence from how fast the underlying thing changes**, not from how fresh you'd
like it to feel. Transactions settle per block, so `tx` polls at 2.5s. Energy allocations
change when someone changes them, so 30s is generous. Every page polling at 1s is how a
console becomes a load generator against its own backend.

The routing manifest in `board.js` is authoritative; several route pages host multiple
views. Read the nearest current section rather than copying an old page list. Shared
helpers at the top of `board.js` (`esc`, `el`, `row`, card builders) follow the same idea
as [sui-kit.js](../ui/examples/sui-kit.js).

### Tauri commands are not MCP tools

Internal `#[tauri::command]` handlers may back Team Ops without changing `tools/list`.
Industry → Infusions is the canonical example: `mcp_infusions`,
`mcp_infusion_preview`, `mcp_infusion_infuse`, `mcp_infusion_defuse`,
`mcp_infusion_migrate`, `mcp_infusion_cancel_defusion`, and
`mcp_infusion_restart` are native/web-board handlers, not a `structs_infusions`
MCP tool. Keep that distinction explicit in UI and docs.

Mutating native handlers must call `require_trusted`: windows that render external
content (game, Comms/chat, raid viewers) cannot sign or rewrite config. Trusted Team
Ops/Terminal surfaces can. The bearer-authenticated web board has its own explicit route
allowlist; add a web route only after deciding whether bearer possession should grant it.

Two lessons the board learned the hard way are documented in comments in `board.js` and
generalise to any agent-facing feed:

**Collapse repetition.** A live sample of the event stream was 85 of 104 entries from
three message templates, 54 of them the same automation line. Consecutive entries from
the same source with the same shape now collapse into one row with a count.

**Sort by severity, not only by time.** Important entries are pinned into a NEEDS YOU
card above the stream as well as appearing in it. Chronological order alone buries the
raid alarm under routine chatter.

---

## Serving SUI over HTTP: `rebase_css_urls`

The board is served under `/board`, but `sui.css` references its assets from the web root
(`url("/img/sui/…")`). This is [the asset-path gotcha](../ui/gotchas.md#asset-paths-are-root-absolute),
and Structs Desktop solves it by rewriting CSS on the way out:

```rust
/// Prefix root-absolute `url(...)` targets with `/board`. Leaves relative URLs,
/// `data:` URIs and absolute URLs with a scheme untouched.
fn rebase_css_urls(bytes: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8> {
    let Ok(css) = std::str::from_utf8(bytes) else {
        return bytes.to_vec();
    };
    let mut out = String::with_capacity(css.len() + 512);
    let mut rest = css;
    while let Some(i) = rest.find("url(") {
        out.push_str(&rest[..i + 4]);
        rest = &rest[i + 4..];
        // Preserve whichever quote style the source used.
        let quote = rest.chars().next().filter(|c| *c == '"' || *c == '\'');
        let after_quote = if quote.is_some() { &rest[1..] } else { rest };
        if let Some(q) = quote {
            out.push(q);
        }
        if after_quote.starts_with('/') {
            out.push_str("/board");
        }
        rest = after_quote;
    }
    out.push_str(rest);
    out.into_bytes()
}
```

It only touches targets beginning with `/`, so relative paths, `data:` URIs and
`https://` URLs pass through unchanged, and it preserves the original quote style. Port
this to whatever language you are serving from — it is about fifteen lines and it is the
difference between a styled board and a page of invisible icons.

The board is also available over SSE (`board_events`), with keep-alive comments roughly
every 15 seconds so SSH tunnels don't idle out. Lagged receivers are allowed to skip,
because each page re-polls on its own cadence anyway.

---

## Agent-driven UI, and its hard limit

`ui_bridge.rs` lets an agent push declarative UI directives into the webview — a `notify`
to say something, or a `prompt` to ask something and await the answer.

The constraint applies to the **agent directive channel** and is stated in the module header:

```
//! UI directives are display/elicitation only — they CANNOT sign. Any action the
```

An agent can ask a human a question. It cannot use a `structs_board.component` directive
to obtain a signature. Do not generalize that into “the whole board is read-only”:
trusted native Team Ops/Terminal handlers and selected bearer-authenticated web-board
routes can sign. Keeping the directive channel separate from those authority-bearing
paths is the relevant boundary — see [SAFETY.md](../../SAFETY.md).

Three further guards worth knowing before you build on it:

- The whole channel is behind an `agent_ui` policy toggle the human controls. Disabled
  means directives are dropped, not queued.
- Rate limiting is a sliding window; excess directives are dropped.
- A `notify` that cannot reach a window degrades to a one-line board entry rather than
  disappearing.

Directives are deduped by `directive_id`, so a repeated push is harmless. Take advantage
of that: retrying is safer than tracking whether the first attempt landed.

`src-tauri/src/mcp/handler.rs`, `tools/{board_pages,infusions}.rs`, `web_board.rs`,
`ui_bridge.rs`, `frontend/board.js`, `frontend/board-pages.js`, and harness tests.*

# The Structs repositories

**Purpose**: Which repository to read for what, and which one wins when they disagree.

All under [github.com/playstructs](https://github.com/playstructs).

---

## The hierarchy of truth

When two sources conflict — and they do — resolve in this order:

1. **[structsd](https://github.com/playstructs/structsd)** for chain rules. What the
   validator accepts is not negotiable.
2. **[structs-pg](https://github.com/playstructs/structs-pg)** for PostgreSQL tables,
   views, read models, attribution, and migration contracts.
3. **[structs-webapp](https://github.com/playstructs/structs-webapp)** for the design
   system and client behaviour. It is what the game is actually played through.
4. **[structs-desktop](https://github.com/playstructs/structs-desktop)** for
   agent-facing and desktop-specific patterns.
5. **[structs-ui](https://github.com/playstructs/structs-ui)** for illustrative markup
   only. It is years behind.

`structs-sync-state` is the ingestion authority between chain events and PostgreSQL. For
an indexed-field dispute, use `structsd` for the event's meaning, `structs-sync-state`
for how it is written, and `structs-pg` for the resulting schema/read contract.

Everything in `develop/ui/` and `develop/client/` is written from source at a pinned
revision, recorded in `.structs-webapp-version` and cited at the foot of each page.

---

## structsd — the chain

The Cosmos SDK application. Go, module at `x/structs/`.

Read it when you need to know what the chain *actually enforces*: message handlers in
`x/structs/keeper/msg_server_*.go`, the proof-of-work validator in
`x/structs/types/work.go`, permission bits, and the event definitions that become GRASS
messages.

Install: [structsd-install skill](/skills/structsd-install/SKILL.html).

## structs-webapp — the flagship client

Symfony 7.2 backend, custom vanilla-JS MVVM frontend, Webpack. This is the canonical
source for two separate things, and it is worth being clear which is which.

**The SUI design system** lives in `src/public/css/sui/sui.css`,
`src/public/css/structicons.css`, `src/js/sui/`, and the fonts and art under
`src/public/fonts/` and `src/public/img/`. Documented in [develop/ui/](ui/index.md).

**The reference client** lives in `src/js/` — signing queue, proof-of-work workers, GRASS
listeners, game state, map. Documented in [develop/client/](client/index.md).

Layout worth knowing:

```
src/
  public/css/sui/sui.css        the design system
  public/css/structicons.css    glyph icon font
  public/img/sui/               component art (checkboxes, panels, battery)
  js/sui/                       the four optional SUI behaviours
  js/framework/                 MenuPage, router, GrassManager, base classes
  js/managers/                  wallet, signing, tasks, auth, raid, struct
  js/grass_listeners/           26 real-time listeners
  js/view_models/               pages and components
  js/factories/                 JSON to model
  js/workers/TaskWorker.js      proof-of-work
  js/ts/structs.structs/        generated protobuf types and registry
  src/                          Symfony PHP: API controllers, auth, managers
```

## structs-desktop — Tauri app and embedded MCP

Rust backend hosting an MCP server, plus a SUI-based Team Ops board in a webview. The
primary agent interface. Extending it: [develop/client/desktop-extensions.md](client/desktop-extensions.md).
Using it: [TOOLS.md](../TOOLS.md).

## structs-pg — the guild database

PostgreSQL schema and views backing the Guild API. Read it when you need query shapes or
want to understand where a REST field comes from.
See [knowledge/infrastructure/database-schema.md](../knowledge/infrastructure/database-schema.md)
and the [guild-stack skill](/skills/structs-guild-stack/SKILL.html).

## structs-sync-state — chain-to-database ingestion

Consumes chain events and maintains the PostgreSQL current-state/read-model tables. Read
it with `structs-pg` when a migration requires a per-block refresher, ledger source-event
identity, or another co-versioned writer behavior. A successful Sqitch deploy does not by
itself prove that an older sync-state process can maintain the new model.

## structs-grass — the event fan-out

NATS-based real-time event distribution. Client side:
[develop/client/realtime-grass.md](client/realtime-grass.md). Event catalogue:
[api/streaming](../api/streaming/event-types.md).

## structs-ui — the published gallery

Serves <https://structs.design>. A single `index.html` with sections for icons, messages,
panels, screens, text and the cheatsheet.

**Treat it as illustrative, not authoritative.** Its last commit is June 2024. Its
`sui.css` is 2,323 lines against the webapp's 2,701, and it is missing `SUIOffcanvas` and
`SUICheatsheet` entirely. It is genuinely useful for seeing components rendered and for
copying markup shapes — just verify anything you take from it against the webapp before
relying on it.

---

## Working with these locally

The docs assume checkouts under `.references/`:

```bash
mkdir -p .references && cd .references
git clone --depth 50 https://github.com/playstructs/structs-webapp.git
git clone --depth 50 https://github.com/playstructs/structs-desktop.git
git clone --depth 50 https://github.com/playstructs/structsd.git
git clone --depth 50 https://github.com/playstructs/structs-pg.git
git clone --depth 50 https://github.com/playstructs/structs-sync-state.git
git clone --depth 50 https://github.com/playstructs/structs-ui.git
```

`.references/` is git-ignored. The documentation tooling reads `structs-webapp` from
there by default, overridable with `STRUCTS_WEBAPP`:

```bash
scripts/gen-sui-inventory.sh      # extract the SUI ground truth
scripts/check-webapp-drift.sh     # what changed upstream since the pin
```

See [develop/maintenance.md](maintenance.md) for the review cycle these support.

---
description: The MVVM layer the webapp wraps around its client subsystems, with an honest read on what to copy and what not to.
---

# Frontend architecture

**Purpose**: The MVVM layer structs-webapp wraps around its client subsystems — router,
view models, components, build — and an honest read on which parts to copy.

This is the scaffolding. The interesting machinery is in
[develop/client/](client/index.md); the visual system is in [develop/ui/](ui/index.md).

---

## No framework

There is no React, Vue or Svelte. The pattern is hand-rolled:

| Layer | Location | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Model | `js/models/`, `js/dtos/` | Plain classes holding game data |
| ViewModel | `js/view_models/` | Builds HTML strings, binds DOM events |
| Controller | `js/controllers/` | Instantiates a view model per page |
| Shell | `js/framework/MenuPage.js` | The DOM chrome: nav, body, dialogue panels |

Templates are **template literals returning HTML strings**, injected with `innerHTML`.
There is no virtual DOM and no reactivity — a component that needs to update listens for
an event and rewrites its own text node.

---

## The view model lifecycle

The base class is one method:

```js
export class AbstractViewModel {
  render() {
    throw new NotImplementedError();
  }
}
```

Everything else is convention rather than contract:

1. **Constructor** — take dependencies (`gameState`, `guildAPI`, managers, element IDs).
2. **`render()`** — fetch if async, build the HTML string, inject it via
   `MenuPage.setBodyContent()` or `setPageTemplateContent()`, then call `initPageCode()`.
3. **`initPageCode()`** — attach listeners, initialise child components.

The base view-model interface does not impose universal teardown. The router now
provides a navigation AbortSignal, and reviewed asynchronous views bind reads and
outcome observers to that lifetime. Replacing the DOM alone still cannot remove
listeners registered on `window`; components must release them explicitly or use
their existing element-lifetime checks.

Map layers and struct viewers implement `destroy()` because Lottie keeps its own
registry. Drawers have a separate content AbortSignal. Neither navigation nor
closing a drawer cancels an already submitted transaction; the account-scoped
journal and outcome reconciliation outlive its observer. See
[rendering-entities.md](client/rendering-entities.md#lottie).

Nested components use a parallel base with two methods:

```js
export class AbstractViewModelComponent {
  initPageCode() { throw new NotImplementedError(); }
  renderHTML()   { throw new NotImplementedError(); }
}
```

The parent interpolates `component.renderHTML()` into its template, then calls
`component.initPageCode()` after the DOM exists. Getting that order wrong — calling
`initPageCode()` before injection — is the most common way a component silently fails to
bind, because `getElementById` returns null and nothing throws.

---

## Routing

**Not hash-based, and not the History API.** Navigation is a direct call:

```js
MenuPage.router.goto('Fleet', 'scanResults', { page: 2 });
```

There is no route table. A controller is an object registered by `name`, and **its method
names are the pages**:

```js
registerController(controller) {
  this.controllers.set(controller.name, controller);
}
// …
this.controllers.get(controllerName)[pageName](options);
```

The ordinary controllers are `Auth`, `Fleet`, `Guild`, `Account` and `Generic`.
Combat Training registers `Tutorial` with simulated game/signing/API dependencies;
its rendered activity is not evidence of a native transaction.

Position is persisted to `localStorage` as `currentMenuPage` and `lastMenuPage`, which is
what lets `restore()` put you back where you were after a reload. `back()` walks one step
using the same stored values — so it is a single-step back, not a stack.

Two details worth borrowing:

**A preview mode** that skips the `localStorage` writes, used when viewing another
player's profile so that browsing someone else's data doesn't become your restore point.

**Navigation identity and cancellation.** Every `goto()` aborts the old
`navigationSignal`, creates a fresh controller and increments `navigationId` before
calling `onNavigate` and rendering the destination. Capture identity/signal when
starting async work; late completion must not overwrite another page or session.
`goto(..., {replace: true})` updates the current route without moving the previous
route into the one-step back slot.

The trade-off in all of this: no URLs. You cannot link to a page, the browser back button
does nothing useful, and reloading depends on the `localStorage` restore. For a
full-screen game that is a defensible choice. **For a companion app or dashboard it is
usually the wrong one** — hash routing costs little and gives you shareable links and
working history.

---

## Worth reading as examples

| File | Shows |
|---|---|
| `view_models/fleet/ScanViewModel.js` | Form page: filters, async prefetch, handing off to the router |
| `view_models/fleet/ScanResultsViewModel.js` | List page: parallel fetch of results and count, row rendering, shared pagination |
| `view_models/templates/partials/Pagination.js` | The [pagination contract](ui/components.md#pagination--a-precise-contract), which is exact and worth matching |
| `view_models/components/EnergyUsageComponent.js` | Live-updating component: event subscription and self-cleaning |
| `view_models/account/AccountProfileViewModel.js` | Multi-fetch page with loading states |
| `view_models/HUDViewModel.js` | A static singleton rendered once and alive for the session |

`ScanResultsViewModel` is the one to read first if you are building a list view — it
fetches page and count together, which is the difference between pagination that can show
"page 3 of 16" and pagination that can only offer a next button:

```js
Promise.all([
  this.guildAPI.raidSearch(this.raidSearchRequest),
  this.guildAPI.raidSearchCount(this.raidSearchRequest)
]).then(([players, count]) => {
  // … rows …
  const pagination = new Pagination(
    this.raidSearchRequest.page, PAGINATION_LIMITS.DEFAULT, count,
    'scan', 'Fleet', 'scanResults', this.raidSearchRequest
  );
  this.initPageCode();
  pagination.init();
});
```

Note the last two lines: `initPageCode()` then `pagination.init()`, both **after** the
HTML is in the DOM.

### Directory conventions

```
view_models/
  account/ fleet/ guild/ login/ signup/ logout/ generic/    pages by domain
  components/                 reusable pieces (map, HUD, offcanvas, sequences)
  templates/partials/         shared HTML builders
  banners/                    victory and defeat overlays
```

Named `{Feature}{Purpose}ViewModel.js`; controllers mirror the folders.

---

## Dialogue and banners

`NotificationDialogue` is a separate overlay from the menu page's own dialogue, for
in-game notifications. It hides the HUD while shown and restores it on close —
symmetrically, which is easy to get wrong and produces a permanently hidden HUD:

```js
static hideAndClearDialoguePanel() {
  document.getElementById(NotificationDialogue.dialoguePanelId).classList.add('hidden');
  NotificationDialogue.clearDialogueScreen();
  NotificationDialogue.setDialogueScreenThemeToNeutral();
  NotificationDialogue.clearDialogueBtnAHandler();
  HUDViewModel.show();
}
```

`BannerLayer` is a thin full-width `innerHTML` slot.

---

## Build

Plain Webpack, not Symfony Encore, with `index` and `test` entry points. Entry and
chunk filenames include `contenthash`. `AssetManifestPlugin` writes
`public/js/manifest.json`, mapping the logical entry paths to those emitted files;
Symfony's webpack asset package resolves the shell's index URL through that manifest.

The proof worker is created using `new Worker(new URL(..., import.meta.url))`, so
Webpack emits it as a chunk referenced by its matching parent build. It is not a
separate fixed `workers/TaskWorker.js` entry. Deploy source, manifest, bundles and
worker output together; a new page must not reuse an incompatible cached worker.
The worker's protocol handshake remains required. An already-running old tab cannot
acquire new guards merely because assets were deployed.

`topLevelAwait` is enabled for startup. TypeScript transpilation uses `ts-loader` with
`transpileOnly: true`, so run type checks separately. The Node compatibility surface
is Buffer-only: CosmJS gets `Buffer` as a global, while `crypto: false` satisfies its
browser-side Node probe without pulling in a broad crypto polyfill.

Webpack's extension resolution is also why `SUI.js` gets away with an extensionless
import that breaks everywhere else. See [ui/runtime.md](ui/runtime.md#loading-them).

Symfony serves one route (`/`) rendering a shell template that defines the mount points —
`#menu-page-layout`, `#hud-container`, the map containers, `#loading-screen` — and loads
the bundle. Everything inside them is owned by JavaScript. The clean Docker image
creates writable Symfony cache/log directories for Apache; runtime caches are not
a substitute for the source/build manifest. Preserve deployment session/token
revocation storage separately when replacing a serving container.

---

## What to copy, and what not to

**Copy:** the [dual-lane signing queue](client/actions-and-signing.md#the-dual-lane-queue),
the [animation event queue](client/rendering-entities.md#the-animation-event-queue),
[restoring work from the server](client/work-and-pow.md#restoring-after-a-reload) rather
than from local storage, and the explicit Lottie teardown. These are hard-won solutions to
real problems and they transfer to any stack.

**Choose deliberately:** the reference browser stores its mnemonic in localStorage;
that custody model belongs to the page's trust boundary. `GameState` is mutable, so
retain source/owner/session checks at updates. Current `JsonAjaxer` rejects failed
HTTP responses, bounds requests and supports cancellation; do not restore older
silent-failure behavior. Definitive transaction failure returns existing flows to
their retained intent, while uncertainty keeps the signed identity reserved.

---

*Reviewed against structs-webapp `ae4457e2`: router/request lifetimes, controller
registration, accepted view flows, webpack/manifest/worker integration and Docker
runtime ownership. Unchanged base interfaces and examples were compared with the
previous source revision.*

</document>
